docs.title: Chapter 1: Process Control Fundamentals
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Remember: Define process control, identify the four elements of a control loop, and name the three modes of a PID controller
  • Understand: Explain why control is needed in industrial processes and how feedback eliminates offset
  • Apply: Trace a complete control loop in a simple process (e.g., level control on a tank) and identify each element's role
  • Analyze: Distinguish between feedback and feedforward control and determine when each is appropriate

docs.title: 1.1 Why Process Control Exists
docs.text:
Every industrial process — a refinery distillation column, a power plant boiler, a pharmaceutical bioreactor — has variables that must stay within defined bounds for the process to produce the right product safely and economically. Temperature too high: catalyst degrades. Pressure too low: vapor pockets form. Flow unsteady: product quality wanders.

Left alone, processes drift. Ambient temperature changes. Feed composition fluctuates. Equipment ages. Process control is the engineering discipline that fights this drift: it continuously measures what's happening, compares it to what should happen, and makes corrections — automatically, without a human adjusting a valve by hand thousands of times per shift.

The final element that makes the correction physical — that translates a control signal into a change in flow — is almost always a valve. This is why Applied Control's portfolio is at the center of every process control system: our products are the hands that actually move.

docs.title: 1.2 The Four Elements of a Control Loop
docs.text:
Every feedback control loop contains four essential elements:

    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                                                      │
    ▼                                                      │
[PROCESS] ──measured variable──► [SENSOR/TRANSMITTER]      │
                                          │                │
                                    process variable (PV)  │
                                          │                │
                                          ▼                │
                              [CONTROLLER] ◄── set point   │
                                          │                │
                                  control output (CO)       │
                                          │                │
                                          ▼                │
                              [FINAL ELEMENT / VALVE] ──────┘
                              (manipulated variable)
Element What it does Applied Control product Process The system being controlled (reactor, tank, pipe) — Sensor/Transmitter Measures the process variable (flow, pressure, temp, level) Rosemount transmitters Controller Compares PV to setpoint, calculates correction DeltaV DCS Final Element (Valve) Physically changes the manipulated variable (flow) Fisher control valves

The valve is the last mile

A control loop is only as good as its final element. A sticky packing, an oversized valve, or a positioner with excessive deadband will defeat even the best controller tuning. This is why valve diagnostics matter — and why FIELDVUE positioners with online diagnostics change the game.

docs.title: 1.3 Control Variables — What We Measure and What We Manipulate
docs.text:
In any loop, we need to be clear about two things:

  • Controlled variable (CV): What we want to keep at setpoint (e.g., tank level, reactor temperature, pipeline pressure)
  • Manipulated variable (MV): What we adjust to control it (e.g., the flow through the feed valve, the steam flow to the heat exchanger)

The art of process control design is choosing the right manipulated variable — the one that has a fast, direct, and large enough effect on the controlled variable.

Boiler drum level control

CV: Drum water level (measured by DP transmitter or radar gauge) MV: Feed water flow rate (manipulated by a feed water control valve — typically a Fisher ES or HP series valve for high-pressure steam service) Disturbance: Steam demand fluctuations from turbines downstream

docs.title: 1.4 Feedback Control — The Core Idea
docs.text:
Feedback control acts after the process variable has deviated from setpoint. The controller sees the deviation and corrects it.

The error signal drives everything:

$$e(t) = SP - PV$$

Where SP is the setpoint and PV is the measured process variable. The controller's job is to drive e(t) toward zero.

Advantages: - Works even if we don't know exactly why a disturbance occurred - Self-correcting by nature - Handles unmeasured disturbances

Limitation: - Reacts after the fact — there will always be some deviation before correction

docs.title: 1.5 The PID Controller — The Workhorse of Process Control
docs.text: The PID controller is the most common controller in industry. It combines three modes of action:

docs.title: Proportional (P)
docs.text:
The controller output is proportional to the current error. Larger error → bigger correction.

$$CO_P = K_P \cdot e(t)$$

Problem: P-only control leaves a steady-state offset — the error never quite reaches zero because when error = 0, the correction = 0 too, and the process starts drifting again.

docs.title: Integral (I)
docs.text:
The controller output is proportional to the accumulated error over time. If a small error persists, integral action slowly adds correction until it's eliminated.

$$CO_I = K_I \int_0^t e(\tau)\, d\tau$$

Problem: Integral action is slow and can cause integral windup (overshoot) if the valve saturates.

docs.title: Derivative (D)
docs.text:
The controller output is proportional to the rate of change of the error. It anticipates where the process is headed and pre-corrects.

$$CO_D = K_D \frac{de(t)}{dt}$$

Problem: Derivative action amplifies sensor noise. Often set to zero for noisy measurements.

Together:

$$CO(t) = K_P \left[ e(t) + \frac{1}{T_I}\int e\,dt + T_D \frac{de}{dt} \right]$$

MicroSim: Adjust P, I, and D gains and watch the process respond. Try the presets to see oscillation, sluggish, and well-tuned responses.

docs.title: 1.6 Feedforward Control — Acting Before the Fact
docs.text:
Feedforward control measures a disturbance and corrects for it before it affects the controlled variable. It's faster than feedback but requires knowing the disturbance in advance.

Feedforward in a heat exchanger

If feed flow rate to a heat exchanger increases (disturbance), a feedforward controller immediately opens the steam valve to add more heat — before the outlet temperature even drops. Feedback control then trims any remaining error.

Fisher valve application: The steam control valve must respond quickly. A FIELDVUE DVC6200 positioner with high-performance tuning and a volume booster gives the fast stroke speeds feedforward control demands.

docs.title: 1.7 Cascade Control — Controller Stacking
docs.text:
In cascade control, the output of an outer (primary) controller becomes the setpoint of an inner (secondary) controller. The inner loop is faster and handles disturbances that would slow the outer loop's response.

[Primary Controller] ──setpoint──► [Secondary Controller] ──output──► [Valve]
     (slow loop)                        (fast loop)

Reactor temperature cascade

  • Primary (outer) loop: Reactor temperature → controls setpoint of steam flow
  • Secondary (inner) loop: Steam flow → directly controls the steam valve position
  • Benefit: If steam header pressure drops, the inner loop instantly compensates before the reactor temperature even notices

docs.text:

Key DeltaV advantages relevant to this chapter:

  • DeltaV CHARMs (I/O): Electronic marshalling eliminates traditional cabinet wiring; I/O assignment changes are software-only
  • HART Integration: DeltaV reads live diagnostics from every FIELDVUE positioner in the plant — friction, signature, travel deviation — without leaving the operator workstation

docs.title: 1.9 Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Process Variable (PV) The measured quantity to be controlled (e.g., level, pressure, temperature, flow) Setpoint (SP) The desired value of the process variable Error The difference between setpoint and process variable: e = SP − PV Manipulated Variable (MV) The quantity adjusted by the controller to bring PV to SP Final Element The physical device that changes the MV; almost always a control valve Dead Time The delay between a change in MV and the first detectable response in PV Offset A persistent difference between SP and PV in proportional-only control Windup Integral accumulation when the controller output is saturated (valve at limits) Cascade A control structure where the output of one controller sets the SP of another

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: Process control exists because industrial processes drift without correction. Every feedback loop has four elements: process, sensor, controller, and final element (valve). The PID controller eliminates error using proportional response (speed), integral action (accuracy), and derivative action (anticipation). Feedforward control adds disturbance rejection speed. Cascade control handles multi-variable processes by nesting faster inner loops. Applied Control provides the final element (Fisher valves) and the control infrastructure (DeltaV DCS) that make these strategies real.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 — Remember

What is the correct order of elements in a standard feedback control loop?

  • A) Controller → Process → Valve → Sensor
  • B) Sensor → Setpoint → Error → Valve
  • C) Process → Sensor/Transmitter → Controller → Final Element (Valve) → Process
  • D) Setpoint → Controller → Sensor → Process

Question 2 — Understand

A proportional-only (P-only) controller is used on a flow control loop. After a setpoint change, the flow settles at 96% of setpoint and stays there permanently. What is the most likely cause?

  • A) The valve has too much friction
  • B) Steady-state offset from P-only control — integral action is needed
  • C) The valve is oversized
  • D) The transmitter is out of calibration

Question 3 — Apply

A customer has a heat exchanger where outlet temperature is too slow to respond to feed flow changes. Which control strategy would most directly improve response speed?

  • A) Increase proportional gain on the temperature controller
  • B) Add derivative action to the temperature controller
  • C) Add feedforward control from feed flow measurement to the steam valve
  • D) Switch to a smaller valve to improve rangeability

docs.title: Ch 2: Fluid Mechanics for Valve Engineers
Chapter 2: Fluid Mechanics for Control Valves
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

  • Remember: State Bernoulli's equation and define the four fluid flow regimes relevant to valve sizing
  • Understand: Explain how pressure drop across a valve creates flow, and why cavitation occurs in liquid service
  • Apply: Calculate Reynolds number and determine whether flow is turbulent or laminar for a given service condition
  • Analyze: Predict when flashing and cavitation will occur using vapor pressure and the cavitation index (sigma)
  • Evaluate: Select the correct Fisher trim option (standard, Cavitrol III, WhisperFlo) based on calculated fluid conditions

docs.title: 2.1 Why Fluid Mechanics Matters to a Valve Salesperson
docs.text:
Every control valve application involves fluid moving through a restriction. Whether you're sizing a Fisher ED for cooling water or specifying a Cavitrol III trim for a de-superheating station, you are applying fluid mechanics — whether you realize it or not.

The physics determines:

  • How much flow a valve passes (Cv, covered in Chapter 5)
  • Whether the fluid will cavitate, erode the trim, and destroy the valve in months
  • How much noise the valve will generate (regulatory and structural concern)
  • Whether special trim is required — and how to justify the premium price

Understanding fluid mechanics is what separates a parts-order salesperson from a trusted technical advisor.

docs.title: 2.2 The Bernoulli Equation — Energy Conservation in Flow
docs.text:
Bernoulli's equation is the foundation of all valve flow theory. It states that in steady, incompressible, frictionless flow, the total energy per unit volume is constant:

$$P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho g z_1 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho g z_2$$

For valves, elevation is usually negligible, so:

$$P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2$$

What this means for a valve: As fluid accelerates through the seat port (vena contracta — the narrowest point of flow), pressure drops. At the vena contracta, velocity is maximum and pressure is minimum. After the vena contracta, flow decelerates and pressure partially recovers.

The Vena Contracta

The vena contracta is the critical point in valve sizing. Pressure at the vena contracta can fall below vapor pressure even when downstream pressure is above vapor pressure. This is where cavitation begins — inside the valve, not downstream.

docs.title: 2.3 Reynolds Number — Turbulent vs. Laminar Flow
docs.text:
The Reynolds number (Re) classifies flow behavior:

$$Re = \frac{\rho v D}{\mu} = \frac{v D}{\nu}$$

Where: - ρ = fluid density (kg/m³) - v = mean flow velocity (m/s) - D = pipe diameter (m) - μ = dynamic viscosity (Pa·s) - ν = kinematic viscosity (m²/s)

Re Range Flow Regime Effect on Valve Re < 2,000 Laminar Cv drops; turbulent Cv tables are invalid; flow is highly viscosity-dependent 2,000–4,000 Transitional Unpredictable; avoid if possible Re > 4,000 Turbulent Standard Cv equations apply; most control valve service

Viscous service is a sizing trap

High-viscosity fluids (heavy crude, molasses, polymer solutions) can easily be in laminar or transitional flow at normal velocities. If you size a valve using standard Cv tables for a viscous fluid, the valve will be undersized — the customer will blame it for not making flow. Always check Reynolds number for viscosity > 20 cP.

IEC 60534 and ISA 75.01 include viscosity correction factors (Fp) for this reason.

docs.title: 2.4 Pressure Drop and the Pressure Profile Through a Valve
docs.text:
Understanding how pressure varies through a valve — not just across it — is essential.

Pressure Profile Through a Globe Valve

P1 (upstream) ───────┐
                      │  ← Pressure recovery (partial)
                      │
                      ├──── Pvc (vena contracta, minimum pressure)
                      │
                      └──── P2 (downstream / back pressure)

Key relationships:
• ΔP = P1 - P2     (overall pressure drop)
• ΔPvc = P1 - Pvc  (drop to vena contracta)
• Pvc < P2         (vena contracta pressure is always lower than P2)

The pressure recovery factor (FL) characterizes how much pressure recovers from vena contracta to outlet:

$$F_L^2 = \frac{\Delta P}{\Delta P_{vc}} = \frac{P_1 - P_2}{P_1 - P_{vc}}$$

Higher FL means less recovery — the vena contracta pressure is closer to downstream pressure. Globe valves have higher FL (0.85–0.95) than ball valves (0.55–0.75), which means globe valves are less prone to cavitation for a given service condition.

docs.title: 2.5 Cavitation — The Valve Killer
docs.text: Cavitation occurs when local pressure drops below the fluid's vapor pressure, forming vapor bubbles. When these bubbles collapse (implode) as pressure recovers downstream of the vena contracta, they release intense shock waves — enough to pit hardened stainless steel.

docs.title: Cavitation Stages
docs.text:
1. Cavitation inception: First bubble formation. Slight noise, no damage yet.
  2. Developed cavitation: Sustained bubble formation and collapse. Crackling/popping sound like gravel in the pipe. Metal erosion begins.
  3. Choked flow: Vapor bubbles fill the vena contracta, limiting flow regardless of how much ΔP increases. Flow is determined by upstream conditions only.

docs.title: The Cavitation Index (Sigma)
docs.text:
The cavitation index (σ) quantifies the risk:

$$\sigma = \frac{P_2 - P_v}{\Delta P}$$

Where: - P₂ = downstream absolute pressure - Pᵥ = fluid vapor pressure at operating temperature - ΔP = P₁ − P₂

Interpretation: - σ >> σᵢ (inception sigma): Safe — no cavitation - σ ≈ σᵢ: Approaching cavitation — consider anti-cavitation trim - σ < σᵢ: Cavitation is occurring — anti-cavitation or multi-stage ΔP required - σ → 0: Approaching choked flow

Each valve style and trim has its own critical sigma value. Fisher publishes σᵢ for each trim option.

MicroSim: Adjust upstream pressure and downstream back-pressure to visualize cavitation onset and the pressure profile through the valve vena contracta.

docs.title: 2.6 Flashing — When Cavitation Doesn't Recover
docs.text:
Flashing occurs when downstream pressure is also below vapor pressure. Unlike cavitation, the vapor bubbles don't collapse — they remain as vapor, and the flow exits the valve as a two-phase mixture.

Effects of flashing: - Dramatic increase in fluid velocity (vapor occupies ~1,600× the volume of liquid water) - Severe erosion from high-velocity two-phase flow - Reduced Cv (two-phase flow requires different sizing equations) - Noise and vibration

Where it occurs: Hot condensate, boiler feedwater recirculation, pressure letdown above saturation temperature.

Mitigation: - Angle body valves (Fisher A31A): direct the high-velocity two-phase flow away from critical surfaces - Hard trim materials: Stellite or ceramic seat/plug faces resist erosion - Low-recovery valve bodies: some globe designs intentionally prevent pressure recovery below downstream Pv

Flashing vs. cavitation — the quick test

If P₂ > Pᵥ → cavitation possible (bubbles collapse) If P₂ < Pᵥ → flashing (bubbles persist into downstream pipe)

docs.title: 2.7 Choked Flow — Maximum Flow Rate
docs.text: Choked flow is the flow rate at which increasing ΔP produces no additional flow. It occurs when the vena contracta velocity reaches the local speed of sound in the fluid.

docs.title: Liquid Choked Flow
docs.text:
$$q_{max} = N_1 F_L C_v \sqrt{\frac{P_1 - F_F P_v}{\rho / \rho_0}}$$

Where FF is the liquid critical pressure ratio factor:

$$F_F = 0.96 - 0.28\sqrt{\frac{P_v}{P_c}}$$

Pc is the thermodynamic critical pressure of the fluid.

What this means practically: Beyond choked flow, the valve cannot deliver more flow no matter how you open it. If a customer says "the valve is wide open but we can't make rate," check whether the process is in choked flow before condemning the valve.

docs.title: Gas/Vapor Choked Flow
docs.text:
For compressible fluids (gases, steam), choked flow occurs at a critical pressure ratio:

$$\frac{P_2}{P_1} \leq \left(\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\right)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}$$

For air (γ = 1.4), this gives a critical ratio of ~0.528. When P₂/P₁ < 0.528, flow is choked and independent of downstream pressure.

docs.title: 2.8 Noise — Hydrodynamic and Aerodynamic
docs.text: Control valve noise is a frequent customer complaint — regulatory, structural, and operator safety concerns.

docs.title: Hydrodynamic Noise (Liquid Service)
docs.text:
• Primary source: cavitation bubble collapse
  • Spectrum peaks at 5–10 kHz
  • Fisher solution: Cavitrol III anti-cavitation trim — drops pressure in stages, preventing bubble formation

docs.title: Aerodynamic Noise (Gas/Steam Service)
docs.text:
• Primary source: jet mixing at vena contracta — turbulent shear generates broadband noise
  • Spectrum peaks at 1–8 kHz
  • Fisher solutions: WhisperFlo and WhisperTrim — multiple small orifices spread the ΔP across many small jets, dramatically reducing noise per IEC 60534-8-3

Calculating noise — the IEC method

IEC 60534-8-4 gives a standardized method for predicting valve noise. The calculation requires: Cv, FL, ΔP, fluid properties, pipe size, and pipe wall thickness.

Fisher's Valvelink software performs this calculation automatically. A valve producing more than 85 dBA at 1 meter requires special consideration for worker safety (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95).

docs.title: 2.9 Compressible Flow — Gas and Steam Sizing
docs.text:
Gases and steam require a different approach because density changes with pressure. Key differences from liquid sizing:

Expansion factor (Y): Accounts for the fact that gas density decreases as it expands through the valve:

$$Y = 1 - \frac{x}{3 F_\gamma x_T}$$

Where: - x = ΔP/P₁ (pressure drop ratio) - xT = pressure drop ratio at choked flow (valve characteristic) - Fγ = ratio of specific heats factor (γ/1.4)

For steam: Use steam tables for density and enthalpy. Superheated steam is treated like an ideal gas with corrections; saturated steam requires special handling to account for the wet/dry boundary.

docs.title: 2.10 Key Fluid Properties for Valve Sizing
docs.text:
Property Symbol Units Where it matters Density ρ kg/m³ All Cv calculations Dynamic viscosity μ Pa·s Reynolds number, viscosity correction Kinematic viscosity ν m²/s Re = vD/ν Vapor pressure Pᵥ bar absolute Cavitation, flashing Critical pressure Pc bar absolute FF factor calculation Specific heat ratio γ — Gas/steam sizing, xT Compressibility factor Z — Real-gas corrections at high pressure

Where to find fluid properties

  • Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook: Comprehensive physical property tables
  • NIST WebBook (webbook.nist.gov): Free online fluid properties database
  • Fisher Valvelink / Emerson Valve Wizard: Pulls properties automatically from REFPROP for common fluids
  • Steam tables: IFC-67 or IAPWS-IF97; built into all valve sizing software

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: Fluid mechanics governs what happens inside every control valve. Bernoulli's equation shows that pressure drops at the vena contracta — the narrowest point — can fall below vapor pressure, triggering cavitation (if P₂ > Pᵥ) or flashing (if P₂ < Pᵥ). The cavitation index (σ) quantifies risk; values below the inception sigma require anti-cavitation trim. Choked flow limits maximum throughput regardless of ΔP. Gas and steam service require expansion factor (Y) corrections. Reynolds number determines whether viscous corrections are needed. These calculations drive the specification of Fisher trim — Cavitrol III for cavitation, WhisperFlo/WhisperTrim for noise — and are the technical basis for commanding premium prices on severe service solutions.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 — Remember

At the vena contracta, what happens to fluid velocity and pressure compared to upstream conditions?

  • A) Velocity decreases; pressure increases
  • B) Velocity increases; pressure decreases
  • C) Velocity and pressure both decrease
  • D) Velocity and pressure are unchanged

Question 2 — Understand

A customer is experiencing crackling/gravel noise in a control valve handling hot water at 160°C. The downstream pressure is 4 bar. The vapor pressure of water at 160°C is 6.2 bar. What is happening, and what is likely needed?

  • A) Aerodynamic noise from high gas velocity — specify WhisperFlo trim
  • B) Flashing — downstream pressure is below vapor pressure; specify an angle body with hard trim (Stellite) or direct the two-phase flow path away from seat
  • C) Cavitation — downstream pressure is above vapor pressure; specify Cavitrol III
  • D) Normal turbulence — no action needed

Rationale: P₂ = 4 bar < Pᵥ = 6.2 bar → flashing, not cavitation.

Question 3 — Apply

Flow through a control valve has stopped increasing despite increasing ΔP. The fluid is liquid water with P₂ = 3.5 bar and Pᵥ = 2.3 bar. What most likely explains this behavior?

  • A) The valve is undersized — increase Cv
  • B) Pipe friction losses are dominating
  • C) Choked flow — the valve has reached maximum flow for current conditions; increasing ΔP beyond the choked condition produces no more flow
  • D) The valve has failed mechanically

docs.title: Sales Implications
docs.text:
Sales bridge — Fluid mechanics to Fisher severe service

Use cavitation and flashing as the opening for premium trim conversations:

  1. Ask: "What fluid, pressure, and temperature?" → If hot liquid or significant pressure drop, always calculate σ.
  2. Compute or estimate σ: If customer's ΔP is large relative to (P₂ − Pᵥ), cavitation is likely. Show them the math — it's persuasive and positions you as the expert.
  3. Quote Cavitrol III proactively: The trim premium is modest; the cost of cavitation damage (unplanned shutdowns, re-trim, replacement) is enormous. Frame it as insurance.
  4. Noise is a safety and regulatory trigger: If your calculation suggests noise > 85 dBA, mention OSHA 1910.95. Plant safety officers respond. This is a conversation engineering management has to join.
  5. "What happened to the last valve in this service?" is the most powerful question you can ask in severe service. The answer almost always justifies special trim — and Applied Control's repair shop can analyze the failed trim and confirm the diagnosis.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Control Valves — Bodies, Trim, and Fisher Products
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

  • Remember: Name the six main control valve body styles and identify their distinguishing characteristics
  • Understand: Explain how valve body and trim selection affects flow capacity, shutoff, noise, and rangeability
  • Apply: Match a valve body type to a given service condition (fluid type, pressure class, ΔP, temperature)
  • Analyze: Evaluate trade-offs between globe, ball, and butterfly valves for a specific application
  • Evaluate: Select appropriate Fisher valve models for common Applied Control customer scenarios

docs.title: 4.1 What a Control Valve Does
docs.text:
A control valve is a variable orifice. By changing the position of a movable element (plug, ball, disk) relative to a fixed seat, it changes the flow area — and therefore the flow rate — through the valve. The amount of flow at a given valve travel depends on three things:

  1. The pressure drop across the valve (ΔP = upstream pressure − downstream pressure)
  2. The fluid properties (density, viscosity, vapor pressure)
  3. The flow coefficient (Cv) of the valve at that travel position

We'll cover Cv and sizing in Chapter 5. This chapter focuses on the physical hardware: body styles, trim configurations, and the Fisher product family.

docs.title: 4.2 Globe Valves — The Control Valve Workhorse
docs.text:
The globe valve is the most common control valve style for throttling service. Fluid enters one side of the body, passes through the seat port (the orifice), and exits the other side. A plug attached to the stem moves up and down to change the flow area.

Why globe valves dominate throttling service:

  • Excellent throttling precision over a wide range of positions
  • Wide choice of trim styles (cage-guided, plug-guided, multi-stage)
  • Best shutoff capability (Class IV, V, VI achievable)
  • Long history of reliable performance in severe service

Trade-offs: - Higher pressure drop in full-open position (compared to ball/butterfly) - Larger, heavier, and more expensive than quarter-turn alternatives - Not ideal for very large line sizes (>12") due to cost

docs.title: Globe Valve Configurations
docs.text:
Single-Port GlobeDouble-Port GlobeAngle Globe Valve

One seat ring, one plug. Simple and easy to maintain. Standard for most throttling applications. The Fisher ED and EZ valves are single-port globe valves.

Best for: General liquid and gas service, moderate ΔP, where shutoff matters

Two seat rings and a plug with two ports. The upward and downward flow forces partially cancel, reducing actuator force requirements for large valve sizes.

Best for: Very large flow requirements where single-port actuator forces would be prohibitive; less common today with high-thrust pneumatic actuators

Flow enters straight and exits at 90°. This allows the valve to function as an elbow, saving piping. Also better for flashing and erosive service — the impingement angle is more manageable.

Best for: Flashing liquids, erosive slurries, where piping layout saves installation cost

docs.title: 4.3 The Fisher Globe Valve Family
docs.text: Applied Control represents the Fisher brand — the world's most widely used control valve line. Here are the core Fisher globe valves you'll encounter:

docs.title: Fisher ED Control Valve
docs.text:
The most versatile general-purpose control valve in the Fisher line.

Attribute Specification Body style Single-port globe, cage-guided trim Size range ½" to 20" Pressure class ANSI 150 to 2500 Temperature range –40°F to +450°F standard; extended with bonnet options Trim options Linear, equal-%, quick-opening, low-flow, anti-cavitation, noise attenuation Shutoff Class IV standard; Class V/VI available Typical service General liquid, gas, and steam; the default choice for most throttling applications

The ED's cage-guided trim is a key advantage — the cage centers the plug throughout travel, giving consistent, stable control even at low travel percentages.

docs.title: Fisher EZ Control Valve
docs.text:
A cost-optimized globe valve for lower-pressure general service.

Attribute Specification Body style Single-port globe, stem-guided Size range ¾" to 6" Pressure class ANSI 150 to 300 Typical service General utility service where a full-featured cage-guided trim is not required

docs.title: Fisher HP Series (High Pressure)
docs.text:
For severe service: high pressure drop, high temperature, or demanding fluids.

Attribute Specification Pressure class ANSI 600 to 4500 Body design Heavier wall, reinforced body for extreme conditions Typical service Steam conditioning, high-pressure gas letdown, supercritical service

docs.title: Fisher Cavitrol III Trim
docs.text:
Not a valve body — a trim option for Fisher ED and similar bodies that addresses cavitation in liquid service.

  • Multi-stage pressure drop: instead of dropping all the pressure at once (causing vapor bubbles to form and collapse violently), the Cavitrol III drops pressure in stages
  • Each stage drops pressure partially, keeping local pressure above vapor pressure throughout
  • Dramatically reduces noise, vibration, and erosion damage

When to specify: Anytime the calculated sigma (cavitation index) falls below the valve's cavitation inception coefficient. Chapter 5 covers the calculation.

docs.title: Fisher Vee-Ball Valve
docs.text:
A segmented ball valve with a V-notch characterized port. Not a globe valve — completely different flow geometry.

  • The V-notch gives an equal-percentage characteristic natively, without needing a shaped plug
  • Excellent for slurry, pulp stock, viscous liquids, and applications where solids pass-through is needed
  • Full line bore in the open position → low pressure drop, easy cleanability

docs.title: 4.4 Ball Valves for Control Service
docs.text:
Quarter-turn ball valves can throttle — but not all of them. A full-bore ball valve at mid-position is a poor throttling valve: most of its flow range is compressed into a small band of travel, and the uncharacterized port gives erratic gain across the range.

For control service, use characterized ball valves:

docs.title: Segmented Ball Valve (V-Notch)
docs.text:
• The Fisher Vee-Ball series
  • V-notch segment replaces full sphere — the notch creates a characterized opening
  • Better rangeability than a full-ball: typically 100:1 vs. 30:1 for a full-bore ball
  • Higher Cv for a given body size than globe valves → compact installations
  • Key market: Pulp and paper, mining, chemical slurries, large-flow liquid control

docs.title: Full-Bore Ball Valve
docs.text:
• Best for on/off isolation; acceptable for slow-throttle applications with limited range requirements
  • Do not use for precise throttling where stable control at 20–60% open is needed
  • Fisher V150/V200 Vee-Ball valves cover control-service ball applications

docs.title: 4.5 Butterfly Valves for Control
docs.text: Butterfly valves use a disk rotating around a central shaft. They are high Cv, low cost, and compact — but require careful selection for throttling.

docs.title: Concentric (Wafer) Butterfly
docs.text:
• Disk and shaft share the same centerline
  • The seat engages the disk eccentrically → poor shutoff (typically Class II)
  • Not suitable for throttling service requiring stable control below ~20% open
  • Use: On/off isolation, large cooling water systems

docs.title: High-Performance Butterfly (HPBV)
docs.text:
• Double-offset disk: the shaft is offset from both the disk centerline and the pipe centerline
  • Better shutoff (Class III–IV), better throttling range
  • Fisher 8580 HPBV series
  • Use: Large line sizes (8"–48"+) where cost of globe valve is prohibitive; utility services

docs.title: Triple-Offset Butterfly
docs.text:
• Third offset: the seating surface is a cone, not a cylinder → zero friction on opening/closing (unlike single and double-offset where the seat drags across the disk)
  • Excellent shutoff (Class V/VI achievable), fire-safe designs, excellent for high-pressure/high-temperature
  • Fisher Vee-Ball V500 and related designs
  • Use: Critical isolation in refining, LNG, high-temperature steam

MicroSim: Drag the stem travel slider to see how plug position, seat port area, and flow rate change in a globe control valve.

docs.title: 4.6 Valve Body Materials
docs.text:
Material selection is driven by fluid chemistry, temperature, and pressure class. Failure to specify correctly leads to corrosion, cracking, or contamination.

Material Common spec Typical service Carbon steel (WCB) ASTM A216 Gr. WCB General service, hydrocarbons, steam to 750°F 316 Stainless Steel (CF8M) ASTM A351 Gr. CF8M Corrosive liquids, food/pharma, aqueous solutions Alloy 20 (CN7M) ASTM A351 Gr. CN7M Sulfuric acid service, highly corrosive chemicals Duplex Stainless (CD4MCu) ASTM A890 Chloride environments, offshore, seawater Hastelloy C (CW6M) ASTM A494 Highly oxidizing acids, aggressive chemicals Bronze ASTM B62 Marine service, low-pressure water

Chloride stress corrosion cracking

Standard 316 SS can stress-crack in hot chloride environments (e.g., produced water in oil & gas). Always ask about chloride content and temperature before specifying stainless. Duplex or Hastelloy may be required.

docs.title: 4.7 Pressure-Temperature (P-T) Ratings
docs.text:
Every valve body has a maximum allowable working pressure (MAWP) at each operating temperature, determined by the body material and ANSI pressure class (ASME B16.34):

ANSI Class Approx. max CWP at 100°F (WCB) Class 150 285 PSIG Class 300 740 PSIG Class 600 1480 PSIG Class 900 2220 PSIG Class 1500 3705 PSIG Class 2500 6170 PSIG

Never derate from pressure alone

Pressure rating drops with temperature. A Class 600 WCB valve rated at 1480 PSIG at 100°F is only rated at ~1050 PSIG at 800°F. Always check the P-T table for the actual operating temperature.

docs.title: 4.8 End Connections
docs.text:
How the valve attaches to the pipe matters for installation, removal, and maintenance:

End connection Notes Flanged (RF or RTJ) Most common for process service; allows easy removal for maintenance Butt-weld (BW) Welded into the line; no flange leakage path; required for high-pressure Class 900+ Socket-weld (SW) Small sizes (½"–2") in high-pressure service Screwed/Threaded (NPT) Small utility valves; avoid for process service where removal matters Wafer Butterfly valves sandwiched between flanges; compact but not suitable for high line forces

docs.title: 4.9 Valve Leakage Classes (ANSI FCI 70-2)
docs.text:
Not all valves shut off equally. The leakage class defines the maximum allowable leak at full close, critical for applications where even small leakage causes safety, environmental, or process problems.

Class Max leakage Typical application Class I No test required On/off valves not requiring tight shutoff Class II 0.5% of rated Cv General throttling where leakage is acceptable Class III 0.1% of rated Cv Moderate leakage requirement Class IV 0.01% of rated Cv Standard for Fisher globe valves; most throttling service Class V 0.0005 mL/min/psi ΔP/in seat Tight shutoff; soft or lapped metal seats Class VI Bubble-tight (per test procedure) Cryogenic, toxic, critical isolation; requires soft seat

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: Control valves are variable orifices — the physical final element of every control loop. Globe valves dominate throttling service because of their precise controllability, wide trim options, and excellent shutoff capability. Fisher ED and EZ valves cover most general-purpose applications; Fisher HP serves severe service. Ball valves (Fisher Vee-Ball) compete for large-flow, slurry, and liquid applications. Butterfly valves shine in large line sizes where globe valve cost is prohibitive. Body material follows fluid chemistry; pressure class follows operating conditions. Leakage class specifies shutoff quality.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Valve Sizing and Flow Coefficients
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

  • Remember: State the definition of Cv and the basic liquid sizing equation
  • Understand: Explain why the same Cv can pass different flows depending on fluid properties and phase
  • Apply: Calculate required Cv for a liquid, gas, and steam service using IEC 60534 equations
  • Analyze: Determine whether a service condition requires anti-cavitation trim or noise attenuation
  • Evaluate: Select the appropriate Fisher valve model and trim for a given sized Cv and service severity

docs.title: 5.1 The Flow Coefficient — Cv
docs.text:
The flow coefficient (Cv) is the universal language of valve sizing. It is defined as:

The number of US gallons per minute of water (60°F) that flows through a valve at a pressure drop of 1 PSI.

$$C_v = q \sqrt{\frac{\rho / \rho_0}{\Delta P}}$$

Where: - q = volumetric flow rate (GPM for liquid) - ρ/ρ₀ = specific gravity relative to water (dimensionless) - ΔP = pressure drop across fully open valve (PSID)

Why Cv works: It captures the valve's physical geometry (seat size, travel, trim shape) in a single number that can be used across all fluids and pressures. Fisher publishes Cv tables for every travel position of every valve model, allowing accurate sizing.

Cv is not Kv

The European equivalent is Kv (flow in m³/h of water at 1 bar ΔP). Conversion: Cv = 1.156 × Kv. IEC documents use Kv; ISA documents use Cv. Fisher publishes both.

docs.title: 5.2 Liquid Sizing — The Full IEC 60534 Equation
docs.text:
For non-choked, turbulent liquid flow (the most common case):

$$C_v = \frac{q}{N_1 F_P} \sqrt{\frac{G_f}{\Delta P}}$$

For choked flow (when ΔP > ΔPchoked):

$$C_v = \frac{q}{N_1 F_P F_L} \sqrt{\frac{G_f}{P_1 - F_F P_v}}$$

Where:

Symbol Description Typical value N₁ Numerical constant (depends on units) 0.0865 (m³/h, bar) or 1.0 (GPM, PSI) FP Piping geometry factor (reducers, etc.) 0.95–1.0 FL Liquid pressure recovery factor 0.85–0.95 for globe Gf Specific gravity of liquid (water = 1.0) Process-dependent FF Critical pressure ratio factor ≈ 0.96 − 0.28√(Pᵥ/Pc)

Practical liquid sizing procedure:

  1. Get: flow rate, inlet pressure, outlet pressure, fluid, temperature
  2. Look up or calculate: Gf, Pᵥ at temperature, Pc (if cavitation possible)
  3. Check if ΔP > ΔPchoked (choked condition); use appropriate equation
  4. Solve for required Cv
  5. Select valve with installed Cv ≥ required Cv at desired travel (typically 70–80% open)
  6. Verify: rangeability, installed characteristic, leakage class

docs.title: 5.3 Gas and Vapor Sizing
docs.text:
Gases and vapors are compressible — density changes with pressure. IEC 60534 uses the expansion factor Y to account for this.

For non-choked gas flow:

$$C_v = \frac{q}{N_9 F_P P_1 Y} \sqrt{\frac{M T_1 Z}{x}}$$

For choked gas flow (when x ≥ Fγ xT):

$$C_v = \frac{q}{N_9 F_P P_1 \cdot 0.667} \sqrt{\frac{M T_1 Z}{F_\gamma x_T}}$$

Where:

Symbol Description x Pressure drop ratio = ΔP/P₁ Y Expansion factor = 1 − x/(3Fγ xT) xT Pressure drop ratio at choked flow (valve-specific) Fγ Ratio of specific heats factor = γ/1.4 M Molecular weight of gas T₁ Inlet temperature (K) Z Compressibility factor (1.0 for ideal gas) N₉ Numerical constant (units-dependent)

Gas sizing: always check for choked flow

For high-pressure gas letdown (regulators, pressure control valves on gas lines), choked flow is common. If you use the non-choked equation in a choked condition, you will specify a valve that is too small.

docs.title: 5.4 Steam Sizing
docs.text:
Steam sizing depends on whether the steam is superheated (treat as gas) or saturated (use steam tables):

Superheated steam (same form as gas, using specific volume from steam tables):

$$C_v = \frac{W}{N_6 F_P Y \sqrt{x P_1 \rho_1}}$$

Where: - W = mass flow rate (kg/h or lb/h) - N₆ = numerical constant - ρ₁ = density at inlet (from steam tables, kg/m³)

Saturated steam: Must use steam table properties at the saturation line. Never assume ideal gas for saturated steam.

Fisher Valvelink / Emerson Valve Wizard

In practice, Fisher's sizing software handles all fluid property lookups automatically. Enter the service conditions and the software returns the required Cv, checks for cavitation, calculates noise, and generates a sizing report. The sales engineer's job is to understand what the software is doing and explain it to the customer — not to do all calculations by hand.

docs.title: 5.5 Flow Characteristics — Installed vs. Inherent
docs.text: The flow characteristic describes how Cv changes with valve travel. It's not how much flow passes — it's the shape of the curve.

docs.title: Inherent Characteristics
docs.text:
Characteristic Cv formula Shape Linear Cv = Cv_max × t Straight line Equal-percentage Cv = Cv_max × Rⁱ⁻¹ Exponential (R = rangeability, typically 50) Quick-opening Cv = Cv_max × √t Square-root curve

Where t = travel as a fraction (0 to 1).

Equal-percentage is the most common choice for throttling service. It provides constant process gain when the valve is the dominant pressure drop in the system.

Linear is correct when the valve pressure drop is constant fraction of system ΔP.

Quick-opening is for on/off service where a large flow area is needed immediately on opening (safety relief bypass, on/off control).

docs.title: Installed Characteristics
docs.text:
The installed characteristic is what the valve actually does in the piping system, which differs from the inherent characteristic because system ΔP changes with flow. The distortion is captured by the valve authority (β):

$$\beta = \frac{\Delta P_{valve, full flow}}{\Delta P_{system, full flow}}$$

  • β > 0.25: installed ≈ inherent (good control)
  • β < 0.1: severe distortion; consider linear trim or resizing

MicroSim: Compare inherent flow characteristics and see how system authority distorts the installed curve.

docs.title: 5.6 Rangeability
docs.text:
Rangeability is the ratio of maximum to minimum controllable Cv:

$$R = \frac{Cv_{max}}{Cv_{min}}$$

Valve type Typical rangeability Globe (cage-guided, Fisher ED) 50:1 Globe (stem-guided, Fisher EZ) 30:1 V-notch ball (Fisher Vee-Ball) 100:1 Butterfly (concentric) 10:1 High-performance butterfly 20:1

Low rangeability means the valve cannot control well at low flow rates — it jumps from closed to significant flow with small stem movement. This causes hunting and instability at low loads.

docs.title: Anti-Cavitation Sizing
docs.text:
When calculated σ < σ_i (inception sigma from Fisher catalog), specify Cavitrol III trim:

  1. The multi-stage trim drops pressure in steps: each stage drops pressure by a small amount
  2. After each stage, pressure recovers slightly before the next drop
  3. At no point does local pressure fall below vapor pressure
  4. The Fisher Cavitrol III is available in 2-stage (moderate) and 3-stage (severe) configurations

Sizing impact: Cavitrol III has lower Cv than standard trim for the same body size. Size the valve body assuming Cavitrol III Cv, then select body size.

docs.title: Noise Calculation and WhisperFlo Selection
docs.text:
IEC 60534-8-3 (aerodynamic noise) and IEC 60534-8-4 (hydrodynamic noise) provide standardized methods. The result is sound pressure level (dB) at 1 meter downstream.

If calculated noise > 85 dBA: specify WhisperFlo or WhisperTrim If calculated noise > 95 dBA: consider multi-stage trim or staged pressure reduction

Fisher Whisper noise attenuation trims: Multiple small orifices break a single high-velocity jet into many small jets. Noise ∝ velocity⁶; reducing jet velocity by half cuts noise by 18 dB.

docs.title: 5.9 Sizing Example — Worked Problem
docs.text:
Service: Cooling water - Flow: 200 GPM at normal; 250 GPM maximum - Inlet pressure: 80 PSIG - Outlet pressure: 45 PSIG (normal), 40 PSIG (maximum) - Fluid: Water at 70°F (Gf = 1.0, Pᵥ = 0.36 PSIA) - Required leakage: Class IV

Step 1 — Normal Cv:

$$C_v = \frac{200}{1.0} \sqrt{\frac{1.0}{80 - 45}} = 200 \times \sqrt{\frac{1}{35}} = 200 \times 0.169 = 33.8$$

Step 2 — Maximum Cv:

$$C_v = \frac{250}{1.0} \sqrt{\frac{1.0}{80 - 40}} = 250 \times \sqrt{\frac{1}{40}} = 250 \times 0.158 = 39.5$$

Step 3 — Check cavitation:

$$\sigma = \frac{P_2 - P_v}{\Delta P} = \frac{45 - 0.36}{35} = \frac{44.64}{35} = 1.28$$

For a Fisher ED, σᵢ ≈ 0.8 — since σ = 1.28 > σᵢ, no cavitation expected.

Step 4 — Select valve:

Required Cv_max = 39.5. Fisher ED 3" Class 150 has rated Cv = 68 at full open. At 70% travel, Cv ≈ 43. → Select 3" Fisher ED, Class 150, equal-percentage trim, Class IV shutoff.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: Valve sizing is the process of matching a valve's Cv to the process requirements. Cv is the universal sizing coefficient: GPM of water at 1 PSI ΔP. IEC 60534 equations extend this to liquids (with viscosity and cavitation corrections), gases (with expansion factor Y and molecular weight), and steam (using steam table properties). Flow characteristics — linear, equal-percentage, quick-opening — determine how Cv changes with travel; installed characteristics depend on system authority. Rangeability defines the controllable flow range. When service conditions indicate cavitation, specify Cavitrol III; for noise, specify WhisperFlo. Fisher's Valvelink software automates these calculations — the engineer's role is to understand the inputs and interpret the output.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 — Remember

Cv is defined as the number of US GPM of water that flows through a valve at what pressure drop?

  • A) 5 PSID
  • B) 1 PSID
  • C) 10 PSID
  • D) 0.1 PSID

Question 2 — Apply

A gas application has P₁ = 100 PSIG, P₂ = 40 PSIG, so x = 60/114.7 = 0.523. If xT for the valve is 0.64 and Fγ = 1.0, is the flow choked?

  • A) Yes — because P₂ < P₁
  • B) No — because x (0.523) < Fγ × xT (0.64), so flow is not choked yet
  • C) Yes — because x > 0.5 for any gas
  • D) Cannot determine without fluid molecular weight

Question 3 — Evaluate

A customer is sizing a valve for hot water at 180°C. Vapor pressure at that temperature is 10.0 bar abs. Upstream pressure is 18 bar, downstream is 6 bar. What do you recommend?

  • A) Standard Fisher ED with equal-percentage trim
  • B) Check sigma: σ = (6 - 10)/12 = −0.33 < 0 — this is FLASHING, not cavitation. Specify angle body valve with hard trim (Stellite/ceramic) directed to handle two-phase flow, or multi-stage pressure reduction upstream.
  • C) Fisher Cavitrol III trim is sufficient
  • D) High-performance butterfly valve

docs.title: Sales Implications
docs.text:
Sales bridge — Sizing to specification

  1. Offer to size it for them. "Send me your data sheet and I'll run it through Valvelink." This positions Applied Control as a partner, not a catalog order desk. A customer who depends on your sizing expertise is a loyal customer.
  2. Document severe service in writing. When your sizing calculation shows cavitation or excessive noise, put it in the quote. If the customer chooses standard trim anyway to save money and the valve fails, you have documented that you recommended the correct solution.
  3. Show the cost of undersizing vs. oversizing. An undersized valve can't make rate — production loss. An oversized valve operates near closed — poor control, stem wear, packing leakage. Correct sizing is not just technical — it's an economic argument.
  4. Rangeability as a differentiator: Fisher ED's 50:1 rangeability vs. a competitor's 20:1 for the same body size is a specific, auditable advantage. Translate it: "Your minimum controllable flow is 2% vs. 5% of rated — that's 2.5× better turndown."

docs.title: Chapter 9: Actuators and Positioners — Moving the Valve
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

  • Remember: Name the three main actuator types and state which is most common in process control
  • Understand: Explain how a spring-diaphragm actuator produces force and why fail-safe action matters
  • Apply: Select the correct actuator size for a given valve thrust requirement
  • Analyze: Interpret a FIELDVUE DVC6200 valve signature and identify what it reveals about valve health
  • Evaluate: Justify the premium cost of a DVC6200 vs. a conventional positioner using diagnostic and loop performance benefits

docs.title: 9.1 The Actuator's Job
docs.text:
The actuator is the muscle of the control valve assembly. It converts the controller's output signal (typically 4–20 mA or pneumatic 3–15 PSIG) into mechanical force and motion — moving the plug, ball, or disk to the position commanded by the controller.

Three requirements an actuator must meet: 1. Sufficient force to stroke the valve against process differential pressure, packing friction, and spring loads 2. Sufficient speed to respond to the process loop's demand 3. Correct fail-safe action — the position the valve moves to on loss of signal or supply

docs.title: 9.2 Pneumatic Actuators — The Industry Standard
docs.text: Pneumatic actuators dominate process control because: - Instrument air is always available in process plants - Spring-diaphragm design is simple, reliable, and self-contained - Inherently fail-safe (spring return on signal loss) - No electrical hazardous area classification required - Force output scales simply with diaphragm area × pressure

docs.title: Fisher 657 Diaphragm Actuator (Spring-to-Open)
docs.text:
The Fisher 657 is the world's most widely deployed pneumatic actuator. It is a spring-to-open, signal-to-close design:

Feature Specification Action Diaphragm case pressurizes → stem moves down (push-down-to-close) Fail action Air fail: spring pushes stem up → valve opens on air failure Spring range 3–15 PSIG, 6–30 PSIG, or custom Sizes 30, 34, 40, 46, 60, 70, 80, 100 in² effective diaphragm area Stroke Up to 4" standard; up to 6" extended Temperature –40°F to +150°F (actuator air space)

Actuator sizing — thrust calculation:

$$F_{required} = F_{packing} + F_{seat} + F_{stem} + F_{unbalance}$$

Where: - F_packing = packing friction (empirical; depends on packing style and stem diameter) - F_seat = seating load required for the specified leakage class (Class V/VI > Class IV) - F_stem = stem area × ΔP (for balanced vs. unbalanced trim) - F_unbalance = differential pressure force across trim if unbalanced design

Fisher's actuator sizing software (ValveLink) performs this calculation and selects the smallest actuator size that meets force requirements with margin.

docs.title: Fisher 667 Diaphragm Actuator (Spring-to-Close)
docs.text:
The Fisher 667 is the spring-to-close, signal-to-open variant:

  • Air pressure pushes stem up → valve opens
  • Air failure → spring pushes stem down → valve closes
  • Correct for fail-closed applications: emergency shutoff, fuel valves, high-pressure gas letdown

Fail-safe selection guide:

Service Preferred fail position Actuator type Fuel or combustion air Fail-closed Fisher 667 (spring-to-close) Coolant/cooling water Fail-open Fisher 657 (spring-to-open) Level control (overflow risk) Fail-closed Fisher 667 Steam to reboiler Fail-closed Fisher 667 Safety system isolation Depends on SIL analysis Per SIL calculation

docs.title: 9.3 Electric Actuators
docs.text:
Electric actuators use an electric motor driving through a gearbox to position the valve. They are preferred when: - No instrument air is available (remote sites, offshore platforms, buildings) - Very precise position control is needed (pharmaceutical batch processes) - High thrust is required without a large pneumatic supply (large gate/globe valves)

Fisher EIM electric actuators cover torques up to 150,000 in-lb for large quarter-turn valves. Features include: - Integral position feedback (potentiometer or encoder) - Limit switches for open/closed position - Handwheel for manual operation during maintenance - HART or FOUNDATION Fieldbus communication options

Trade-offs vs. pneumatic: - Slower stroke speed (seconds to minutes vs. sub-second for pneumatic) - More complex maintenance (motor, gearbox, controls) - Higher purchase cost for comparable thrust - Excellent for slow processes (temperature, large vessel level)

docs.title: 9.4 Hydraulic Actuators
docs.text:
Hydraulic actuators use pressurized oil (typically 1,500–3,000 PSIG) to produce very high force in a compact package. Used for: - Extremely large valves (choke valves, large gate valves, pipeline mainline isolation) - High-cycle rate applications (compressor anti-surge) - Remote deep-sea or high-temperature installations

Fisher YD series hydraulic actuators provide stroke forces up to 100,000 lbf for large subsea valves. Not common in general process plant service.

docs.title: 9.5 Positioners — Closing the Position Loop
docs.text:
A positioner is a local feedback controller that compares the commanded position (from the DCS, 4–20 mA) with the actual position (from the stem position feedback) and modulates the actuating pressure to eliminate any position error.

Without a positioner: The 4–20 mA signal directly loads a current-to-pneumatic (I/P) converter, which sets actuator pressure. Packing friction, supply pressure variations, and stem force changes cause position errors.

With a positioner: The positioner continuously corrects for all of these — it knows where the valve actually is and drives the actuator until the position matches the command.

docs.title: Why Positioners Are Now Standard
docs.text:
On legacy systems, positioners were sometimes omitted to save cost. Today they are standard because:

  1. Tighter control: Position error < 0.5% of span vs. 5–10% without positioner
  2. Diagnostics: Modern positioners (DVC6200) report position, friction, signature, and alert on deviation — impossible without feedback
  3. Split-range control: Two valves controlled on different parts of the 4–20 mA signal requires positioners
  4. HART communication: Enables remote access to valve health data from the DCS workstation

docs.title: 9.6 Fisher FIELDVUE DVC6200 — The Digital Valve Controller
docs.text: The DVC6200 is the flagship positioner from Fisher — the most sophisticated, most widely deployed intelligent positioner in the industry.

docs.title: Key Specifications
docs.text: Attribute Specification Input signal 4–20 mA HART (standard) or 4–20 mA with HART Feedback Hall-effect travel sensor (contactless, non-wearing) Supply pressure 1.4–10.0 bar (20–145 PSIG) Temperature –40°C to +85°C (–40°F to +185°F) Hazardous area ATEX II 2G, FM Explosionproof, CSA Communication HART Revision 5/7; optional FOUNDATION Fieldbus, PROFIBUS Diagnostics Full valve signature, friction trend, travel deviation, alert history Mounting Direct-mount to Fisher actuators; universal for third-party

docs.title: DVC6200 Diagnostic Capabilities
docs.text:
This is what separates the DVC6200 from any conventional positioner:

1. Valve Signature (Stroke Test) The DVC6200 can perform an automated stroke test while the valve is in service (for non-critical loops) or offline. It records: - Supply pressure - Actuator pressure - Valve travel ...at every point through the full stroke. The resulting signature reveals:

  • Packing friction: Width of the hysteresis loop in the signature
  • Seat condition: Abnormal force signature near seating
  • Actuator spring rate: Slope of the signature — detects spring failure
  • Diaphragm leakage: Pressure hold test identifies air leaks

2. Travel Deviation Alert If the actual valve position deviates from commanded position by more than a set threshold, the DVC6200 raises a Hart alert visible in the DCS or AMS Device Manager. This catches: - Packing sticking - Plug-seat contact preventing full close - Actuator pressure loss

3. Friction Trending The DVC6200 tracks friction over time. A rising friction trend indicates packing wear before it causes control problems. Schedule the maintenance before the failure — not after.

4. Partial Stroke Testing (PST) for SIS For safety-instrumented system valves, the DVC6200 can perform a partial stroke test — moving the valve 10–15% from the fully open position to prove mechanical integrity without disrupting process flow. Required by IEC 61511 for SIL 2 and SIL 3 applications to achieve proof test coverage targets.

Accessing DVC6200 diagnostics

DVC6200 diagnostics are accessed through: - HART handheld (375/475 Field Communicator): For field technicians during commissioning - Emerson AMS Device Manager: Plant-wide asset management; historical trending; alert management - Emerson DeltaV with DVC6200 integration: Real-time HART reads into the DCS historian; alerts appear on operator displays - ValveLink software: Dedicated valve management application; generates PDF reports for compliance documentation

docs.title: 9.7 DVC2000 — Entry-Level Smart Positioner
docs.text:
For less critical service or tighter budgets, the Fisher DVC2000 provides HART communication and basic diagnostics at lower cost:

  • Integral to actuator mounting (direct mount only)
  • HART communication for remote position readout
  • Basic friction and travel deviation alerts
  • No full valve signature capability
  • Appropriate for general process service where signature analysis is not required

docs.title: 9.8 Volume Boosters and Accessories
docs.text:
For fast-stroking applications (anti-surge, emergency shutdown), the positioner's output may not drive actuator pressure fast enough. Volume boosters solve this:

  • A volume booster amplifies the positioner's pilot signal with a high-flow relay
  • The actuator fills and exhausts at high flow rates (fast stroke)
  • The positioner controls precisely, the booster provides the flow capacity
  • Fisher 627 Series volume boosters: flow capacity up to 300 SCFM at 100 PSIG

Accessory ecosystem:

Accessory Function Volume booster Fast stroke speed Trip valve Pneumatic on/off override (ESD) Solenoid valve Electrical on/off isolation of air supply Supply regulator Filters and regulates instrument air to clean, constant pressure Lock-up valve Locks valve position on air supply failure (preserves last position) Limit switches Position feedback to DCS as discrete signal Position transmitter 4–20 mA position feedback to DCS

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: Actuators are the muscle of the control valve assembly. Fisher 657 (spring-to-open) and 667 (spring-to-close) diaphragm actuators cover the vast majority of process control applications; fail-safe action is a critical selection criterion. Positioners close the position feedback loop, eliminating errors from packing friction and supply pressure variation. The Fisher DVC6200 FIELDVUE positioner is the industry benchmark — not just for position control precision, but for its diagnostic capabilities: valve signature, friction trending, travel deviation alerts, and partial stroke testing. These diagnostics reduce unplanned downtime, justify maintenance scheduling, and enable SIS proof testing. The DVC6200 is Applied Control's strongest single product for proving value to a plant's maintenance and reliability organization.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 — Remember

What is the fail-safe action of a Fisher 657 spring-diaphragm actuator?

  • A) Fail-closed (spring drives stem down on air failure)
  • B) Fail-open (spring drives stem up on air failure — with push-down-to-close trim)
  • C) Lock in last position
  • D) Depends on supply pressure

Question 2 — Understand

A control valve's hysteresis is 8% of span (very high). Without a positioner, what does this mean for loop control?

  • A) The loop will control tightly — the DCS will compensate
  • B) The valve will stick and jump — small controller output changes produce no movement, then a large position jump; the loop will hunt and oscillate
  • C) The loop gain will be reduced, making the loop sluggish but stable
  • D) The positioner senses this automatically and corrects it

Question 3 — Evaluate

A plant maintenance manager says: "We can't justify the DVC6200 premium over a basic positioner — the valve works fine." What is the strongest single response?

  • A) The DVC6200 has better position accuracy
  • B) It has a HART address for AMS integration
  • C) "The DVC6200 can detect a valve that is 'working fine' but slowly building friction — before it fails. One avoided unplanned shutdown typically pays for the entire positioner budget across a year. Can you show me the last time this valve was pulled and inspected?"
  • D) It meets the latest HART revision requirements

docs.title: Sales Implications
docs.text:
Sales bridge — Actuators and positioners to plant value

  1. The positioner is the data source. Every DVC6200 is a sensor that reports valve health. Position it not as a "box on the actuator" but as the plant's window into its most critical final elements.
  2. Lead with reliability, not features. The maintenance manager doesn't care about HART Revision 7. They care about: How many unplanned shutdowns did we have last year, and how many were valve-related? The DVC6200 answers that question before the next shutdown.
  3. The upgrade conversation is easy. A plant with old pneumatic-only positioners has zero diagnostic visibility into ~50% of its valves. A DVC6200 retrofit requires no new wiring (4-20 mA HART rides on the same pair) and takes 2 hours per valve. ROI is typically less than one avoided maintenance call.
  4. Partial stroke testing is a regulatory driver. For any SIL 2+ safety valve, IEC 61511 requires documented proof tests. PST with the DVC6200 is the lowest-disruption method. Cite the standard when talking to the safety engineer — it closes.
  5. Applied Control's valve shop + DVC6200 = closed loop. We can install the DVC6200, capture a baseline signature, store it in AMS, and compare it 12 months later. If friction doubled, we schedule a shop rebuild. The customer never has a surprise failure.

docs.title: 18.1 What Makes Applied Control Different
docs.text:
Applied Control is not a distributor. It is an Emerson Impact Partner — one of a select tier of regional specialists who provide not just products but engineering expertise, field service, and lifecycle support. Understanding this distinction is the foundation of every sales conversation.

The Applied Control value proposition:

Competitor claims Applied Control delivers "We carry Fisher" We are Fisher experts — certified repair, sizing, configuration "We have the part" We have the engineering knowledge to ensure it's the right part "24-hour delivery" 24-hour delivery and the expert who knows if it will work "Competitive pricing" Lower lifetime cost through correct sizing and preventive diagnostics

The five pillars of Applied Control differentiation:

  1. Fisher valve expertise — The deepest Fisher product knowledge in the region, from standard ED/EZ to severe service and specialty trim
  2. National Board Certified valve shop — Repair, remanufacture, and certify Fisher valves and pressure relief valves to as-new specification
  3. FIELDVUE diagnostics — Baseline, trend, and analyze every valve in the plant using DVC6200 and AMS Device Manager
  4. DeltaV system integration — Full Emerson DCS/SIS design, configuration, and commissioning capability
  5. Local presence, Emerson depth — Same-day field service backed by Emerson's global supply chain, engineering resources, and 24/7 support line

docs.title: Phase 1: Territory Mapping
docs.text:
Before calling on accounts, map the territory:

  • Who are the large industrial users? (refinery, chemical plant, power generation, water treatment, food/beverage, pharmaceutical)
  • What is the installed base? Fisher valves already in the plant are immediate maintenance, upgrade, and diagnostic opportunities
  • Who are the key decision-makers? Plant manager (P&L), maintenance supervisor (reliability), process engineer (performance), safety manager (SIS compliance), purchasing (price)

Applied Control CRM: Every customer site, every valve population, every planned outage and turnaround should be in the CRM. The sales process begins months before the customer calls.

docs.title: Phase 2: Discovery
docs.text:
Discovery is the most important phase. The goal is to understand problems the customer hasn't stated yet.

The five discovery questions (for any plant visit):

  1. "How are your control loops performing — any hunting, oscillation, or offset?" → Opens positioner upgrade, packing replacement, valve diagnostic conversation

  2. "When did you last have an unplanned shutdown related to a valve or instrument?" → Opens reliability, DVC6200 diagnostics, valve shop discussion

  3. "Are you planning any turnarounds or outages in the next 6–18 months?" → Opens proactive repair, spare parts, remanufacture conversation

  4. "What standards are you under for your safety instrumented functions?" → Opens DeltaV SIS, IEC 61511, partial stroke testing conversation

  5. "What does your vendor relationship look like for DCS support?" → Opens DeltaV migration or support contract conversation

Listen for pain, not for product fit. Don't pitch until you understand the problem.

docs.title: Phase 3: Technical Qualification
docs.text:
Once a problem is identified, apply technical depth to define the solution:

  • Get the P&ID, data sheet, or service record
  • Size the valve or positioner correctly (don't guess)
  • Calculate cavitation index if liquid service with significant ΔP
  • Calculate noise level for gas/steam service
  • Determine actuator thrust from stem force requirements
  • Specify the correct Fisher model, body size, trim, leakage class, actuator, positioner

This is where subject matter expertise closes the deal. A competitor who quotes from a catalog cannot match a proposal that includes sizing calculations, cavitation analysis, and a documented justification for each specification choice.

docs.title: Phase 4: Proposal and Business Case
docs.text:
Every significant proposal should include:

  1. Technical specification — What we recommend and why (from the sizing/analysis)
  2. Business case / TCO — Why it costs less over the life of the asset (see Section 18.4)
  3. Applied Control differentiators — Specifically why Applied Control over a generic distributor
  4. Risk statement — What happens if the alternative (cheaper) solution is chosen

docs.title: Phase 5: Lifecycle Engagement
docs.text:
The sale doesn't end at the PO. The relationship deepens after installation:

  • Baseline valve signature after installation (DVC6200)
  • Annual diagnostic review — friction trends, alert history, recommendations
  • Turnaround support — Applied Control field service team on-site during outages
  • AMS Device Manager report — Semi-annual or annual valve population health report

A customer who receives a diagnostic report every year sees Applied Control as a partner, not a vendor. This creates loyalty that no competitor can easily displace with a 10% price reduction.

docs.text:

Maintenance Supervisor Reliability, predictability "DVC6200 diagnostics tell you a valve is failing 3 months before it fails." docs.title: 18.4 Total Cost of Ownership — The TCO Argument
docs.text:
TCO analysis is the most powerful tool for justifying Fisher vs. generic alternatives. Build it with real numbers whenever possible.

TCO elements for a control valve:

Cost category Generic alternative Fisher ED + DVC6200 Purchase price Lower Higher (+15–30%) Installation Similar Similar Diagnostics None (additional analyzer needed) Included in DVC6200 Maintenance frequency Reactive (avg. 2.5 yr cycle) Predictive (avg. 4.5 yr cycle based on signature) Unplanned downtime cost 1 event/5 yr avg. 0.2 events/5 yr avg. with DVC6200 Trim replacement (cavitation) Every 12–18 months (unprotected) Every 5+ years (Cavitrol III protected) Repair labor Internal + contractor Applied Control valve shop (faster turnaround) Energy loss (leakage) Class II (0.5% Cv) Class IV (0.01% Cv) — 50× less leakage

Example TCO calculation:

A chemical plant has 50 control valves. Average unplanned shutdown cost: $120,000. Probability of valve-caused shutdown without diagnostics: 1 per year. With DVC6200 diagnostics: 0.2 per year.

Annual risk reduction = (1.0 - 0.2) × $120,000 = $96,000/year
DVC6200 upgrade cost (50 valves) = $125,000
Payback period = $125,000 / $96,000 = 1.3 years
10-year NPV of diagnostic investment: > $700,000

Present this math, not a brochure.

The sales engineer who can solve the customer's problem before the customer knows they have it is the sales engineer who will never lose a deal on price.
